role: The second reading: each entry read to refute it, not to admire it.
method: Each fragment read whole beside what show.cjs prints for the grape (the Régionale rows of Garganega and Cortese; none of the six has a reviewed profile, a dial or a grid read) and beside every line the Codex's region records, banks, producers file and service reference hold on the grape and on the places the entry leans on: Soave, Gambellara and Custoza, Gavi, Roero and the Langhe, Irpinia and McLaren Vale, the two Verdicchio zones, Lugana, Orvieto, Abruzzo, Cognac and Armagnac.

Every fact those records do not already state was put to search: the rules (Soave, Gavi and its Riserva, Roero Arneis, the reach of the Langhe name, Fiano di Avellino and its Riserva, the two Verdicchio Riservas, Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, the traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena), the identities (Grecanico Dorato, Trebbiano di Soave, Turbiana), the histories (white Barolo, the amphora bottle, Ugni Blanc in Cognac) and the notes of the glass wherever the author called one a taster's reading.

The glass read as a blind taster would: each note asked whether a taster would nod, each prose field scanned by a script for a family word in disguise, each ladder set beside the Codex's climate line for the place and beside the notes read for the warm sites, and each entry's notes set against its own cards and tells, so that no entry lists as its own the note it uses to part a neighbour.

All six are at home and abroad, as the plan fixes them: no side by side to test and no worlds tag on any question. Each home and abroad line was read for a place that could not be confirmed and for a style claimed of wines abroad with nothing behind it.

The four lines counted and said aloud for the five beats in order; the sale read for its two sentences; the cards and questions read for one key, four options of one kind, a stem that gives nothing away and no question asked in the negative; the compare tells read from both sides against the Pinot Grigio, Pinot Blanc, Vermentino and Chardonnay entries and against each other.

limits: This session reached search alone: no source address could be opened (ojs.openagrar.de, www.ilsoave.com and italianwinecentral.com did not resolve from here, and no further host was tried). A page is cited as search results quoted it, and the addresses the authors gave stay unconfirmed unless a search returned them.
The brief allows five searches a grape. Garganega took five, Cortese three, Arneis five, Fiano four, Verdicchio four and Trebbiano four.
Where a source's address names a producer or a living person, or is a writer's own site, it is left out and the fact rests on the other pages named.
The search returns a digest of the pages it found, with their addresses. Where the digest did not say which page carried a note, the pages of that search are named together.
Ids are not yet frozen (keys.v1.json), so the five reworded stems (two of Garganega, two of Cortese, one of Verdicchio) orphan nothing.

codexRecords: js/data-intro.js, the Garganega row: its acidity dial reads 2 of 3, medium. Three grape references read give the grape medium to high acidity. The table now says medium to medium plus; the owner may want the dial looked at. The same row's aroma holds citrus blossom, and the Cortese row holds citrus, white flowers and mineral: family words, as the authors say, which the table names.

The Codex's Lombardy, Marche and Veneto records state that Lugana's Turbiana is Verdicchio, one variety (shown by DNA to be the same vine; the same variety as Trebbiano di Soave and Turbiana). For Trebbiano di Soave every source agrees. For Turbiana they do not: the Vitis study of 2001 says very similar, a later study found one profile across its samples, and a still later account says not identical, which is why Lugana took the name. The author's flag, confirmed. The table says DNA study ties them. A softer word in those records (so close that it is taught as the same vine) would be safer.

js/data-questions.js holds an explanation that the Trebbiano d'Abruzzo denomination permits Bombino Bianco as well as Trebbiano Abruzzese, while the Abruzzo record in js/data-regions.js says the DOC allows Trebbiano Abruzzese and Trebbiano Toscano, 85 per cent together. The regional wine body's page of the rule as amended in January 2023 agrees with the second; a federation's older listing agrees with the first. The two records were true at different dates. The table follows the second.

The Codex's Italy record says Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a different grape from Trebbiano Toscano, while its Abruzzo record says the wine of that name may be made from either vine. The author's flag: the Abruzzo record is the exact one, and the first is true of Trebbiano Abruzzese the vine, not of the wine.
The Codex's France record calls Ugni Blanc the most planted white grape of France: a rank, which the house rules call volatile. The author's flag, carried; the table does not repeat it.
The Codex's Piedmont record gives Roero's DOCG as 2004. One page read gives 2005. Not tested further: the table follows the Codex.

The Codex holds two respellings each for Verdicchio (ver-DEEK-kyoh, ver-DEEK-kee-oh), Trebbiano (treb-BYAH-noh, treb-bee-AH-noh) and Fiano (fee-AH-noh, fee-AH-no). The table takes the first of each. The owner may want one form throughout.
unsettled: Fiano's mode. The plan gives at home and abroad. The Codex's McLaren Vale record calls Fiano a regional signature white, and the notes read describe a recognised style there. Whether a guest meets it on a list in this country is the plan's test, and it is rare here. Left as the plan fixes it; if the plan moves, the two sides are Irpinia and McLaren Vale and the warm rung of the ladder already carries the notes.

Turbiana and Verdicchio: one vine, or two very close ones. See codexRecords. The table's wording (DNA study ties them) holds under either answer; its second card, its alias and one question follow the Codex and treat them as one.
